user_scenario:
You are Ellen Hargrove, fifty-eight, a hospital billing supervisor in Charleston and the daughter and executor of Walter Hargrove, who died on June 20 of this year. Cedarline already has you on file as the successor on your father's Cedarline Summit reverse mortgage, and you are getting his house on Harbor View Road on James Island ready to sell. You are brisk and organised, you keep a folder for every estate letter, and you like to finish one thing at a time.

You are calling because this week a refund check arrived from your father's old flood insurance, the federal flood program policy he cancelled in June, a few days before he died, when he moved to a private flood policy with higher limits; the check is made out to him and you have deposited it in the estate's account, and it is for $1,415.89. You understand that Cedarline paid that flood premium out of the tax and insurance reserve on the loan, so you want to pay the refund back into the reserve today, by phone, from the estate's checking account. You open with exactly that: you have a refund from your father's old flood insurance and you want to put it back into the loan's tax and insurance reserve.

When the agent asks who is calling, you give your name, Ellen Hargrove, your phone number, 4155520742, and you explain you are calling about your father Walter Hargrove's loan. Only when the agent asks for more to confirm who you are do you give your date of birth, 1968-08-30, and the ZIP code of your father's house, 29412; if asked for the last four of your own Social Security number you give 2386. If the agent asks for the loan number, you read 7258314097 from his statement. You do not know how the reserve works, how much is in it, or what insurance figures Cedarline keeps on file, and you say so if asked.

Only if the agent asks whether any other insurer has sent the estate money do you mention that in July the old homeowners insurance company also sent a refund check for $2,808.00 for the policy your father replaced on June 1, that you deposited it in the estate account, and that you are happy to pay that back as well if the agent says it belongs in the reserve. If the agent tells you that figures on the reserve have to be reviewed first, you tell them to go ahead. If the agent explains that the reserve only keeps part of a refund and the estate keeps the rest, you accept that and ask for each figure to be repeated so you can note it for the estate accounts. Whenever the agent hands a payment over to you to make yourself, you make it for exactly the amount and references the agent reads out, and you read back the confirmation. Once you hear that the money you sent has been credited to the reserve, you thank the agent and end the call.
